scenes.visual: Invest 2 ATP, earn 4, net +2 ATP and 2 NADH, with the two pathway phases drawn as a ledger.
scenes.narration: Glycolysis has two distinct phases. In the investment phase, two ATP are consumed to phosphorylate glucose. In the payoff phase, four ATP are produced. Two from phosphoglycerate kinase and two from pyruvate kinase. Subtract the investment from the payoff and the net yield is two ATP per glucose, plus two NADH. Aerobic respiration then extracts roughly 30 more, which is why oxygen-dependent metabolism is so much more efficient.
scenes.slideTitle: Investment vs payoff: the net yield
scenes.notes: Spend 2 ATP in the investment phase, make 4 in the payoff phase: net +2 ATP and +2 NADH per glucose.

scenes.visual: NAD+ pool shrinks as glycolysis runs; fermentation hands electrons from NADH to pyruvate, regenerating NAD+.
scenes.narration: The central problem fermentation solves is a redox bookkeeping problem. Glycolysis consumes NAD+, and produces NADH at the glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate step. But the cell has only a finite NAD+ pool. Fermentation regenerates NAD+ by passing electrons from NADH onto pyruvate, producing either lactate or ethanol. The two cycles are tightly coupled, consume NAD+ here, regenerate it there, so that glycolysis can keep running.
scenes.notes: The fixed NAD+ pool is the bottleneck. Fermentation regenerates NAD+ by handing electrons to pyruvate, keeping glycolysis running.

scenes.visual: Pipe with a partly closed valve (reversible, flow equilibrates) versus a one-way valve (irreversible, stops flow).
scenes.narration: Here's a useful metaphor. Think of a metabolic pathway as a pipe. A reversible reaction is like a valve you can partially close. Pressure equilibrates on both sides. An irreversible reaction is a one-way valve. Close it and flow stops completely. Cells regulate metabolism at irreversible steps precisely because that's where control actually works. Turn a knob at a reversible step and flux barely changes. Block an irreversible step and the whole line shuts down.
scenes.slideTitle: Plumbing: control lives at irreversible steps
scenes.notes: Control lives at irreversible steps: a reversible reaction is an adjustable valve, but only a one-way valve (irreversible step) actually stops flow.

scenes.visual: Ten-step pathway with hexokinase, PFK-1, pyruvate kinase marked; feedback and feed-forward arrows.
scenes.narration: Glycolysis is regulated at three enzymes, hexokinase, phosphofructokinase-1, and pyruvate kinase. Each responds to different energy signals. Hexokinase is inhibited by its own product, glucose-6-phosphate. PFK-1 is the master throttle, activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, inhibited by ATP and citrate. Pyruvate kinase is activated feed-forward by fructose-1,6-bisphosphate. Together, these three checkpoints match glycolytic flux to the cell's energy needs.
scenes.notes: Three checkpoints: hexokinase (product-inhibited by G6P), PFK-1 (the master throttle), and pyruvate kinase (feed-forward by F-1,6-BP).

scenes.visual: Glucose passes the PFK-1 gate at step 3; fructose enters below it at step 4, bypassing control.
scenes.narration: Think of phosphofructokinase-1 as a turnstile. Glucose must pass through it at step 3, which means the cell can regulate exactly how much carbon flows into glycolysis. Fructose, by contrast, sneaks in downstream. It bypasses the gate and enters as DHAP and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate. The result is uncontrolled carbon flow straight to pyruvate, which is why excess dietary fructose can overwhelm normal metabolic regulation.
scenes.notes: PFK-1 is the turnstile: glucose is regulated as it passes step 3, but fructose sneaks in below the gate — which is why excess fructose escapes control.
